 “The ball is in Mr. Cruz’s court,” Clancy’s defense attorney said of Plymouth District Attorney Tim Cruz.
 By Abby Patkin

 Livestream via NBC10 Boston. 
 Lindsay Clancy is due back in court Monday, with lawyers on both sides expected to discuss when — and how — she could potentially be retried for killing her children. 
 More than two months after the Duxbury mother’s murder trial ended in a hung jury, Plymouth District Attorney Tim Cruz has yet to outline his plans for the case moving forward. Prosecutors have suggested they are eyeing a retrial, though Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said earlier this month “what that looks like will depend.”
 Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has chafed against the uncertainty, demanding to know why prosecutors have not yet decided whether to retry Clancy on first-degree murder, reduce her charges, or resolve the case some other way. 
 Advertisement: “I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three,” Reddington told Judge William Sullivan during a Nov. 2 hearing. “I want a trial, and I want it with you, and I want it this spring.”
 More on Lindsay Clancy:
 Judge denies Lindsay Clancy’s motion to dismiss murder charges 
 Lindsay Clancy case: It was a contentious day in court. Here’s what happened. 
 Florida woman charged with wiretapping Lindsay Clancy’s former father-in-law 
 Clancy, 36, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan. While she has not denied strangling her children at home in Duxbury on Jan. 24, 2023, Clancy raised what is commonly known as an insanity defense as she maintains she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and heard a voice in her head ordering her to kill the children and herself.
 Advertisement: Her high-profile murder trial ended in a mistrial Sept. 4 amid reports of a holdout juror who refused to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility for the killings. That juror, Michael Desronvil, has repeatedly said he had no doubt about Clancy’s guilt. However, Desronvil’s jury service quickly came under scrutiny following allegations regarding his personal legal troubles and phone use during deliberations. 
 Clancy’s defense argued unsuccessfully that her charges must be dismissed because Sullivan should have done more to investigate whether Desronvil was fit to remain on the jury in light of notes from the foreperson indicating he was refusing to follow instructions on reasonable doubt. Sullivan denied that motion to dismiss last week, though Martin G. Weinberg, an appellate expert and member of Clancy’s defense team, told Boston.com he expects an appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court in the “very near future.”
 Sullivan also denied two more motions last week, including a defense request to launch an inquiry into the holdout juror and prosecutors’ motion to place a gag order on Reddington. 
 Monday’s hearing will serve as a status or trial assignment conference, Sullivan previously said. The judge has floated the idea of a March retrial, while Reddington has suggested April. 
 Advertisement: “The ball is in Mr. Cruz’s court,” Reddington said Nov. 2, gesturing toward the district attorney in the courtroom gallery.
 Abby Patkin 
 Staff Writer 
 Abby Patkin is a general assignment news reporter whose work touches on public transit, crime, health, and everything in between. She has been covering the Lindsay Clancy murder case since January 2023.
